readerTitle: Why "we clean for everyone" brings in no one
caseNote: 가상 사례 두 개 (가정 청소 업체, 회사 안의 교육팀) · 수치는 설명용
insight: 마케팅은 모두에게 말하는 일이 아니라, 한 무리를 골라 그들의 머릿속에 특정한 자리를 잡는 일이다.
misconception: 고객을 좁히면 시장이 작아져 손해다. 모두에게 알리는 메시지가 가장 많은 고객을 데려온다.

sources.text: 마케팅 교과서의 표준 개념 (세분화·표적·포지셔닝, STP). 예: Kotler & Keller, Marketing Management
Ries, A. & Trout, J. (1981). Positioning: The Battle for Your Mind. McGraw-Hill.
청소 업체와 교육팀 사례는 설명용 가상 예시

factChecks.note: 청소 업체와 사내 교육팀은 모두 가상 사례입니다. 마케팅 예산 $2,000은 설명용 가정이며 결과를 수치로 제시하지 않았습니다.
'Positioning' 개념을 Ries & Trout가 대중화했다는 서술과 책 출간 연도(1981)를 게시 전에 확인하세요. 카드 5에서는 'popularized'로만 표현했습니다.
포지셔닝 문장 틀(For [target] who [need], we are the [category] that [difference])은 업계에서 널리 쓰이는 형식이며 특정 출처의 인용이 아닙니다.

cards.title: Why "we clean for everyone" brings in no one
body: A small cleaning company prints a flyer: "Homes, offices, move-outs, deep cleans. We do it all!" Few people call.
Across town, a training team inside a large company emails every employee: "New courses for everyone!" Few people sign up.
Different worlds, same mistake. Both are talking to everyone, so nobody feels the message is for them.

image.label: A flyer and an email both ignored by passing crowds
image.brief: 화면을 반으로 나눔. 왼쪽은 동네 게시판의 "We do it all!" 전단을 사람들이 그냥 지나침. 오른쪽은 사무실 모니터의 "Courses for everyone!" 이메일을 직원들이 넘김. 따뜻한 플랫 일러스트, 실제 로고 없음.

cards.title: You have $2,000 to market a cleaning business.
body: Maya runs a three-person home cleaning company. She cleans for busy families, for tenants moving out, and sometimes for small offices.
She has $2,000 for marketing this season. What should she do with it?

options.text: Spread it across ads that show every service, so no customer is missed
options.feedback: She reaches the most people, but each sees a vague message. $2,000 split many ways is too thin to stand out with anyone.

options.text: Pick one group, like tenants moving out, and build the message around their problem
options.feedback: She gives up talking to some customers for now. In return, one group hears a message that sounds written just for them.

options.text: Keep the message general but lower prices to beat rivals
options.feedback: Low prices can win calls, but they also cut what each job leaves. And she still hasn't given anyone a reason to pick her besides price.

cards.title: Maya chose the people moving out.
body: Tenants moving out have a deadline, a landlord inspection and a deposit at stake. Families wanting weekly help care about trust and routine. Same service, very different needs.
So Maya aimed at movers. She left flyers with letting agents, offered a cleaning checklist that matched what landlords inspect, and priced by flat size instead of by hour.
Her new line: **"The move-out clean that gets your deposit back."** Calls started coming from agents, not only tenants.

image.label: One market split into three groups, one highlighted
image.brief: 큰 원을 세 조각으로 나눔: "Busy families", "Tenants moving out", "Small offices". "Tenants moving out" 조각만 밝은 색으로 강조하고 열쇠와 체크리스트 아이콘을 넣음.

cards.title: Segment, target, position
body: Maya followed three steps that marketers call **segment, target, position**.

*Segment:* split the market into groups whose needs differ. *Target:* choose the group you will serve best and aim at it first. *Position:* decide the one thing you want that group to think of when they think of you.
For Maya: three segments, one target (movers), one position (the deposit-back clean).

image.label: Three steps: split, choose, claim a place
image.brief: 왼쪽에서 오른쪽으로 3단계 인포그래픽. 1) 사람 무리를 색깔별로 나눔 "Segment" 2) 한 무리에 과녁 표시 "Target" 3) 그 무리의 말풍선 안에 브랜드 자리 하나 "Position". 단순한 아이콘 스타일.

cards.title: Position lives in the customer's head.
body: Positioning, an idea popularized by Al Ries and Jack Trout, is not your slogan. It's the spot you hold in the customer's mind next to the alternatives.
A simple test is to fill in one sentence:
**"For** [target] **who** [need], **we are the** [category] **that** [difference]."
For Maya: for tenants moving out who want their deposit back, we are the cleaning service that cleans to the landlord's checklist. If you can't fill it in, customers can't either.

cards.title: Split by situation, not only by age.
body: Segments based on age or income are easy to draw but often miss the point. The same 35-year-old can be a busy parent in March and a tenant moving out in June.
Groups that share a **situation and a need** usually respond to the same message. They also tend to gather in the same places, like letting agents for movers. That makes them easier to reach.
cards.softwareNote: A project tool might segment by situation: agencies juggling clients, or one team planning a launch. Each needs different onboarding, pricing and examples, even if the product is the same.

cards.title: Narrow on purpose, not by accident.
body: A target segment must be big enough to pay the bills, reachable through channels you can afford, and truly different in what it needs. A segment that fails any test is just a smaller audience.
Targeting also has a cost: some customers will feel the message isn't for them. That's the point, but check you can live with it.
And targeting is where you aim, not who you refuse. Maya still cleans for families who call.

cards.title: Now it's a training team inside a company.
body: You run learning and development at a 2,000-person company. Your new leadership course had weak sign-ups after an all-staff email.
You can relaunch it once. What do you do?

options.text: Send the email again with a stronger subject line to all staff
options.feedback: A better headline helps a little, but the course still speaks to no one in particular. Most staff aren't managers and will skip it again.

options.text: Aim at people promoted to manager in the last year, and pitch it as "your first 90 days leading a team"
options.feedback: You lose the reach of an all-staff blast. You gain a group with an urgent need and a message that names their exact situation.

options.text: Give each department an equal number of seats to be fair
options.feedback: It fills seats evenly, but fair isn't the same as relevant. Some departments may send people who don't need it.

cards.title: Pick who it's for, then claim one clear place in their mind.
body: Split your market by need, choose the group you serve best, and give them one reason to think of you first.
**Try it today:** fill in the sentence for your business: "For ___ who ___, we are the ___ that ___." If the blanks feel vague, your marketing probably does too.
